body_markdown:
In another victory for[the little guy](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/right-to-repair/) , New York is poised to become the first state to ban subscription-based services to hardware already installed in new cars. This week, the state’s governor, Kathy Hochul, signed into law senate bill S9348A, which makes it illegal for auto manufacturers to charge such fees. New York probably won’t be the last state to enact this type of consumer protection, either.


BMW made headlines in 2020 when it announced it was going to start charging subscription fees for features that were already installed during the manufacturing process: heated seats and heated steering wheels, synthesized engine sounds, music partnerships, advanced safety features, automatic high-beam headlights, and navigation, to name a few. You could subscribe by the month, by the year, or buy it outright.


BMW


What a terrible idea! said consumers tired of what they perceived as nickel-and-diming at every turn. What a great idea! said rival carmakers, who recognized the high margins inherent in the software side hustle of the low-margin day job that is building cars. General Motors, for example, has long charged[a subscription fee](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/the-subscription-economy-will-make-drivers-poorer-unless-they-own-a-classic/?_gl=1*2t7m3j*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTk4Nzk2NjY4Mi4xNzk1NDU0ODkx*_ga_C1Z3NGGXZT*czE3OTU1NTc4NjEkbzIkZzAkdDE3OTU1NTc4NjEkajYwJGwwJGgw) for its OnStar safety service and, more recently, for its SuperCruise autonomous driving functionality. That pair of software services alone accounted for $5.4 billion in revenue for the company in 2025.


According to[Business Insider](https://www.businessinsider.com/general-motors-gm-earnings-subscriptions-revenue-business-2026-1) , in a July 2026 earnings call, GM CEO Marry Barra said the company’s software side “keeps roughly 70 cents of every dollar it brings in. That’s a rare level of profitability in the auto industry, as many car sales generate just four to 10 cents per sales dollar.”


Cadillac


BMW and the General are not alone, of course. Ford charges monthly, yearly, or lifetime subscription fees for BlueCruise. Tesla removed the Full Self-Driving (Supervised) from its options list early this year and instead incorporated it into a $99 monthly service, with fees set to increase as the technology improves. Mercedes and Toyota offer their own subscription services.


[New York’s law](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S9348/amendment/A) , which amends the general business law with a new section, goes into effect on February 27, 2027. The justification of the bill, introduced by Senator James Skoufis, is no-nonsense: “Car companies are increasingly charging consumers a subscription fee to access certain features on their vehicles, such as heated seats, entertainment options, enhanced navigation, and hands-free driving, even though the components necessary for such features to function are already installed on the vehicle at the time of sale…


“During this time of rising consumer prices, it is essential to guard against these business practices that hurt New York consumers. By restricting the offering of subscription services or post-purchase fees for features that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers or manufacturers, this bill seeks to enhance transparency in pricing for consumers. This bill aims to establish clear rules prevent exploitative practices as vehicles become more technologically advanced, and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.”


The law says that carmakers and dealers cannot “offer to a consumer[a subscription service](https://www.hagerty.co.uk/articles/subscription-classic-cars/?_gl=1*2t7m3j*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTk4Nzk2NjY4Mi4xNzk1NDU0ODkx*_ga_C1Z3NGGXZT*czE3OTU1NTc4NjEkbzIkZzAkdDE3OTU1NTc4NjEkajYwJGwwJGgw) or charge a post-purchase fee for any motor vehicle feature that: 1) uses components and hardware already installed on the vehicle at the time of purchase, or 2) functions after activation without ongoing cost to the dealer, manufacturer, or any third-party service provider.”


Excluded from the law are services like navigation updates, infotainment features, satellite radio, and WiFi.


While many find it ridiculous to pay for remote start or heated seats already installed in the car, there is a sticking point among manufacturers that incorporate autonomous features into their cars: ongoing costs associated with developing and improving such hands-free driving technology. The bill’s justification above, and the governor’s office, each listed hands-free driving among the gripes associated with subscription fees, but the investments by automakers in this area are significant. That will be something to keep an eye on, not just with the New York law, but as consumer protection advocates in other states inevitably delve into these waters.
